finding.claim: The /settings/email endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. The account-modifying operation has no authentication enforcement. Depending on set_email's handling of a None uid, an anonymous attacker can change the email of a null/unowned account or of records matched by a NULL uid. This can lead to account takeover through the email-based reset flow.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, a state-changing operation on the user's email

trace.note: decorated with login_optional rather than login_required
login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None when there is no session, and never aborts
set_email(g.uid, ...) is called with the possibly-None uid

finding.guards_checked: login_required (lines 8-16) is correctly applied to /settings/password but not to /settings/email. There is no other auth check or CSRF token in the handler. login_optional never rejects. set_email is a stub, so no downstream uid validation is visible.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") and never aborts; no CSRF or other check in change_email)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies login_optional, which at routes.py:22 sets g.uid to None for anonymous users and never aborts, so routes.py:37 calls set_email(None, ...) without authentication, unlike /settings/password at routes.py:42. The impact (account takeover) is speculative because set_email at routes.py:48 is a stub, but the missing authentication on a state-changing endpoint is real.
